deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivation in the strict sense. It holds three lattice/tiling sketches on pre-dotted (triangular-grid) paper and one short, uncertain numerical note.

(1) Upper half, red ink. A large periodic 'zigzag' network drawn on the dot grid. Long segments run diagonally from upper left to lower right. They are joined by vertical segments, so each strand forms a staircase or Z-pattern. The strands are repeated by translation, filling a sheared parallelogram-shaped region. Small circles sit at one kind of corner, apparently where a diagonal meets the lower end of a vertical. Every node has three edges: up/down vertical, left diagonal and right diagonal. The network is therefore combinatorially the honeycomb (hexagonal) graph, drawn in 'brick-wall' or sheared form. Its faces are the parallelogram-like hexagons visible between strands. The circled nodes appear to mark one of the two bipartite sublattices. Equivalently, it reads as an oblique projection of stacked unit cells, a 'staircase' view of a 3D lattice. This would fit the cube-lattice and block drawings on the previous page (f.16r). Near the upper left of the network is a small annotation, perhaps '5' and 'ρ²'. If it is ρ², it suggests the triangular (Eisenstein) lattice Z[ρ], with ρ a primitive cube root of unity, as the lattice the network is built on. This is my interpretation.

(2) Lower left, black ink. A hexagon, slightly irregular and with circled vertices, divided into triangles from an off-centre interior point. Some of these triangles are further subdivided. The small cells are marked with '+' or '·', i.e. a two-colouring of the triangular cells, with a second lighter pencil overlay. This looks like a two-colouring (checkerboard parity) of a triangular subdivision. It might also be a residue/sign pattern on the triangular lattice, cf. the mod-3 digit triangles on f.16r. My interpretation is tentative.

(3) Lower centre, red ink. Two hexagons sharing a vertex region with circled vertices, plus a tail edge descending from one vertex. This is a fragment of the regular honeycomb drawn in standard (non-sheared) form. It is presumably a comparison with the sheared drawing (1), showing that the brick-wall net is the honeycomb. That inference is mine.

(4) Foot of page, upside down. Something like '19 = 6…'. The reading is uncertain. Plausible arithmetic glosses, all mine and unverifiable from the image: 19 = 1 + 6 + 12 (centred hexagonal number, 3·2·3 + 1). Or 19 = 6·3 + 1, i.e. a prime ≡ 1 (mod 3), hence a norm from Z[ρ]: 19 = 5² − 5·2 + 2² = N(5 + 2ρ) with ρ = (−1 + √−3)/2. Either gloss would tie to hexagonal/Eisenstein lattices, but neither can be confirmed.

No computation is carried through on the page.
errors: No derivations to check. The geometric sketches are consistent with the honeycomb graph: three edges per node, bipartite circle-marking. The hexagon in (2) is freehand and irregular, which is not an error of substance.

deep.surprise_reason: These are lattice and tiling doodles: the honeycomb net, a coloured triangulated hexagon, and a fragmentary numerical note. Gauss's interest in plane and space lattices (Seeber review 1831) and in the Eisenstein lattice Z[ρ] for cubic residues is well documented. Nothing here goes beyond routine geometric visualization.

transcription_corrections: The faint annotation near the upper-left of the red lattice is better read as uncertain ('5', possibly 'ρ²' or '5³'); it is very faint.

The black hexagon is divided from an off-centre interior point (right of centre), not strictly from the centre, and some triangles are further subdivided. A lighter pencil overlay with small circles lies inside it.
The upside-down text at the foot is uncertain; it may read '19 = 6·…' or similar, and the second token is not clearly '1'.
The red network is better described as a sheared honeycomb (brick-wall) net with circled nodes on one sublattice, rather than a generic zigzag.
